analysis.title: What does the US-Iran conflict mean for markets?
key_insights: Brent crude fell about 4.5% on 2 November to below USD 110 as Iranian-Qatari talks raised hopes of progress toward ending the conflict. No agreement has been announced.
Brent ended October at its highest level in six months before the Monday drop.
Iranian and Qatari officials held a third day of talks, and Iranian officials described the discussions as ongoing and progressing.
Middle Eastern supply has continued to recover. October exports from Saudi Arabia rose from September despite attacks on regional energy infrastructure.

Flows through the Strait of Hormuz and bypass pipelines have moved closer to pre-conflict levels, but daily volumes remain volatile. UBS says this does not mean the physical oil market has normalized.
Maritime security deteriorated further in October. Elevated insurance, freight and ship-to-ship transfer costs keep raising the delivered cost of oil.
The impact of renewed escalation would depend on targets, breadth and duration, particularly whether attacks stay on military assets or spread to civilian and energy infrastructure.

UBS CIO remains constructive on global equities, citing resilient economic activity, strong corporate earnings and continued AI investment. It advises against a broadly defensive stance on geopolitics alone.
UBS favors broad commodity exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals and agriculture, as diversification and protection against prolonged supply disruption or inflation pressure.

sector_views.rationale: Broad commodity exposure diversifies portfolios and protects against prolonged supply disruption or added inflation pressure from renewed attacks.
Supported by resilient economic activity, strong corporate earnings and continued AI investment.

macro_indicators.reading: below USD 110, down about 4.5% on 2 November
macro_indicators.interpretation: Diplomatic hopes reduced immediate pressure on oil prices, but the physical market remains fragile.
About 2.8 million barrels a day below the level a year earlier.

macro_indicators.indicator: Middle East to Asia crude shipping cost
macro_indicators.interpretation: Compared with less than USD 5 a barrel before the conflict, which raises the delivered cost of oil.

trade_ideas.description: Hold broad commodity exposure across energy, precious metals, industrial metals and agriculture as a hedge against energy disruption and inflation
trade_ideas.rationale: Broad commodity exposure can diversify portfolios and provide protection if renewed attacks cause a prolonged supply disruption or additional inflation pressure.
trade_ideas.risk: Talks could produce an agreement that normalizes energy flows.

risk_factors: Renewed attacks could cause prolonged supply disruption or additional inflation pressure.
Escalation toward civilian and energy infrastructure would be more damaging than attacks focused on military assets.
Daily oil flow volumes through the Strait of Hormuz and bypass pipelines remain volatile.
Higher insurance, freight and ship-to-ship transfer costs raise the delivered cost of oil.

tension_points.bull_case: Iranian-Qatari talks are described as ongoing and progressing, and Saudi October exports rose from September, so supply is recovering.
tension_points.bear_case: No agreement has been announced, flows remain volatile, maritime security worsened in October, and renewed attacks could disrupt supply again.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Renewed attacks, especially on civilian and energy infrastructure, would invalidate the supply recovery thesis.
